1.title: CDMP FUNDAMENTALS
1.text: Welcome to Module 7: Data Security. This is Chapter 7 of the DMBOK, worth about six percent of the exam. Data Security is one of the more intuitive chapters because so much of it maps to ideas you already know — passwords, encryption, firewalls. But the exam tests precise distinctions, like authentication versus authorization, or persistent versus dynamic masking. So let's make sure those distinctions are crisp. Here we go.

1.title: Module Overview & Learning Objectives
1.text: Here's our roadmap. You'll define Data Security and its three goals. You'll learn the Four A's — plus a fifth concept, Entitlement — and the memorable Goldilocks Principle. You'll distinguish the risk classifications and the five confidentiality levels. You'll map the key regulations — SOX, HIPAA, FERPA, PCI-DSS — to their data categories. You'll compare the encryption methods and the types of data masking. And you'll recognize the threats, the malware types, and the five security activities. Let's start with the definition.

1.title: Definition & Goals
1.text: The DMBOK defines Data Security as the planning, development, and execution of security policies and procedures to provide proper authentication, authorization, access, and auditing of data and information assets. Notice those four words — authentication, authorization, access, and auditing — because they're the Four A's we'll return to shortly. There are three goals. First, enable appropriate access while preventing inappropriate access to enterprise data. Second, understand and comply with all relevant regulations and policies for privacy, protection, and confidentiality. And third, ensure the privacy and confidentiality needs of all stakeholders are enforced and audited. So the whole chapter really orbits those Four A's.

1.title: Business Drivers & the Goldilocks Principle
1.text: There are two primary business drivers for data security. The first is risk reduction — meeting regulatory compliance, fulfilling fiduciary responsibility, and protecting reputation. The second is business growth — because trusted, secure e-commerce drives profit, and robust security builds customer confidence. Now, one memorable concept the exam likes: the Goldilocks Principle. It says data security must be appropriate — not too lax, but also not so onerous that it prevents users from doing their legitimate work. Just right. The DMBOK also gives a four-step information security process: identify and classify sensitive data, locate it across the enterprise, determine how each asset needs protecting, and identify how the information interacts with business processes. Remember the Goldilocks Principle: not too much, not too little.

1.title: The 6 Guiding Principles
1.text: Data Security follows six guiding principles. One, collaboration — it involves IT security, data stewards, governance, audit, and legal all working together. Two, an enterprise approach — standards applied consistently across the whole organization, not piecemeal. Three, proactive management — staying dynamic, engaging stakeholders, and overcoming cultural bottlenecks. Four, clear accountability — well-defined roles, including a chain of custody for data. Five, metadata-driven — security classification is an essential part of data definitions, so the classification travels with the data. And six, reduce risk by reducing exposure — minimize the proliferation of sensitive data, especially into non-production environments. The principle the exam most likes to highlight is that security is metadata-driven.

1.title: Essential Concepts — Vulnerability, Threat, Risk
1.text: Three foundational terms, and the exam expects you to tell them apart. A vulnerability is a weakness that allows a successful attack — think unpatched systems, weak passwords, untrained users, or backdoors. A threat is a potential offensive action against the organization; it can be internal or external, malicious or unintentional, and the collection of possible threats is sometimes called the attack surface. And risk is both the possibility of loss and the condition that poses that potential loss. Organizations prioritize risks by factors like probability, the type and amount of damage, the effect on revenue, the cost to fix, the cost to prevent, and the attacker's intent. So in one line: vulnerability is the weakness, threat is the potential action, and risk is the possibility and condition of loss.

1.title: Risk Classifications & the Aggregation Rule
1.text: The DMBOK gives three risk classifications for data. Critical Risk Data, or CRD, is personal information that's aggressively sought, has high direct financial value, and can harm both individuals and the company. High Risk Data, HRD, is actively sought and provides a competitive edge; its exposure causes financial harm and legal exposure. And Moderate Risk Data, MRD, has little tangible value to outsiders, but its unauthorized use still negatively affects the company. So the severity order is CRD, then HRD, then MRD. And here's a crucial rule the exam loves: the aggregation rule. The highest security classification of any single piece of data in a data set determines the classification of the entire set. One critical field drags the whole dataset up to its level.

1.title: The Four A's (+ Entitlement)
1.text: Now the centerpiece, laid out in the four quadrants on screen: the Four A's of security. Access means enabling authorized individuals to connect to information systems in a timely manner. Audit means reviewing security actions and user activity to ensure compliance with regulations and policy. Authentication means validating users' identities — through passwords, tokens, or biometrics — with transmissions encrypted. And Authorization means granting individuals the privileges to access specific data appropriate to their role. There's also a fifth, more recently added concept: Entitlement, which is the sum total of all the data elements exposed to a user by a single access authorization decision. The distinction the exam tests most is authentication versus authorization. Authentication is about who you are — proving your identity. Authorization is about what you're allowed to do. Don't ever swap those two.

1.title: Monitoring — Active vs. Passive
1.text: There are two kinds of security monitoring, and they serve different purposes. Active monitoring happens in real time — it detects unexpected events as they occur and alerts on or interrupts suspicious activity. Think of it as a detection mechanism. Passive monitoring tracks changes by taking snapshots over time and comparing trends against benchmarks. Think of it as an assessment mechanism. So the quick contrast: active monitoring is real-time detection, while passive monitoring is snapshot-based assessment. The exam may give you a scenario and ask which type is being described — listen for "real-time" versus "periodic snapshots."

1.title: The 5 Data Confidentiality Levels
1.text: The DMBOK defines five confidentiality levels, climbing from least to most restrictive as the ladder on screen shows. For General Audiences means it's public — available to anyone. Internal Use Only means it's limited to employees, with minimal risk if shared, but not for copying outside the organization. Confidential means it isn't shared outside the organization without a non-disclosure agreement. Restricted Confidential means access is limited to roles with a genuine need to know, and may require security clearance. And Registered Confidential is the highest level — anyone accessing it must sign a legal agreement. The key rule: any given data set can have only one confidentiality level, and that level is set by the most sensitive item within it. Notice how that mirrors the aggregation rule from a moment ago.

1.title: Confidentiality vs. Regulatory Classification
1.text: This slide draws a distinction the exam genuinely loves, so lock it in. Confidentiality classification originates internally — your organization decides it — and a data set has exactly one confidentiality level. Regulatory classification, on the other hand, is externally defined by laws and regulators, and crucially, it's additive. That means a single data set can carry multiple regulatory categories at the same time — it might be subject to PII rules and financial regulations and health-privacy rules all at once. So the contrast is: confidentiality is internal and singular, while regulatory is external and additive. If a question asks which type of classification can stack multiple categories on one dataset, the answer is regulatory.

1.title: Regulatory Families
1.text: Let's map the major regulations to their data categories. Personally Identifiable Information, or PII, is covered by things like the EU privacy directives, Canada's PIPEDA, Japan's PIP Act, and Gramm-Leach-Bliley. Financially sensitive data is governed by Sarbanes-Oxley, insider trading laws, and GLBA. Personal Health Information, PHI, is protected in the US by HIPAA. Educational records are protected by FERPA — the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act. And payment card data falls under PCI-DSS, the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard. The three you most need to keep straight: HIPAA is health, FERPA is education, and PCI-DSS is payment cards. Those exact mappings show up regularly on the exam.

1.title: SOX vs. Insider Trading Laws
1.text: Here's a small but frequently tested distinction within financial data. Sarbanes-Oxley, SOX, restricts who can change financial data — it's about protecting the integrity and validity of those numbers. Insider trading laws, by contrast, restrict who can see financial data — it's about confidentiality, preventing people from acting on information they shouldn't have. So the one-line memory hook: SOX governs who can change the data, while insider trading laws govern who can see it. Change versus see. The exam will absolutely put both in the answer choices and see if you can tell them apart.

1.title: Encryption — 3 Methods
1.text: Encryption translates plain text into complex codes to hide privileged information, verify a transmission, or verify the sender's identity. There are three main methods, shown side by side on screen. Hashing uses algorithms like MD5 and SHA to convert data into a mathematical representation; it's one-way and used mainly for verifying transmission integrity. Private-key, or symmetric, encryption uses a single key for both encrypting and decrypting — common algorithms include AES, DES, and 3DES. Public-key, or asymmetric, encryption uses a key pair: the sender encrypts with the recipient's public key, and the recipient decrypts with their private key — methods include RSA and Diffie-Hellman, and PGP is a well-known free implementation. The key contrast: symmetric uses one shared key, asymmetric uses a key pair, and hashing is for integrity, not secrecy.

1.title: Data Masking — Persistent vs. Dynamic
1.text: Data masking makes data less available by removing, shuffling, or changing its appearance — but without losing its meaning or relational integrity. There are two main types. Persistent masking, also called static, permanently and irreversibly alters the data; it's used when creating copies for non-production environments, like test or development. Dynamic masking changes only what the end user sees, without altering the underlying stored data — for example, showing a Social Security number as asterisks followed by the last four digits. Persistent masking has two sub-types: in-flight, where data is masked while moving from source to destination — more secure and re-runnable — and in-place, where the source and destination are the same and the unmasked data gets overwritten, which is risky if the process fails partway. Remember: persistent for test copies, dynamic for production display.

1.title: Masking Methods & Tokenization
1.text: The DMBOK lists eight masking methods: substitution, which replaces values from a lookup or pattern; shuffling, which swaps values between rows; temporal variance, which shifts dates by a small number of days; value variance, which applies a random percentage factor; nulling or deleting; randomization; encryption; and expression masking, which sets values to the result of an expression. There's also a ninth, key masking, which ensures the result is unique and repeatable — important for database key fields. Now, related but distinct from masking is tokenization. Tokenization replaces sensitive data with a non-sensitive surrogate, a token, that has no mathematical relationship to the original value — unlike encryption, which is reversible with a key. Tokenization is most commonly used for payment card numbers, because it reduces an organization's PCI-DSS compliance scope. Keep tokenization and encryption separate in your mind.

1.title: Access Control Models
1.text: Let's look at access control models. Role-Based Access Control, RBAC, grants access based on the user's role, and it's the DMBOK's primary approach — typically implemented with a role assignment grid or hierarchy. Attribute-Based Access Control, ABAC, grants access based on policies that evaluate attributes of the subject, the resource, the action, and the environment. Discretionary Access Control, DAC, lets the data owner grant permissions at their own discretion. And Mandatory Access Control, MAC, enforces security labels set centrally by the system. The exam scenario to watch for: when access depends on multiple contextual attributes at once — say, a user's department and the time of day and the data's sensitivity label — the right model is ABAC, because only ABAC evaluates all those attributes together.

1.title: Network Security Terms
1.text: A quick tour of network security terms. A firewall filters network traffic and is the most primitive form of an intrusion prevention system. A DMZ, or de-militarized zone, is an edge area with a firewall on both sides — between the internet and the organization's internal network — used to pass or temporarily hold data moving between organizations. A VPN uses the internet to create an encrypted, secure tunnel into the organization. A backdoor is a hidden entry point that bypasses password requirements, and any backdoor is a security risk. Penetration testing is when an ethical hacker attempts to break in, identifying vulnerabilities before they can be exploited maliciously. And a key logger is attack software that records every keystroke and sends it to a hacker. The one most likely to be tested is the DMZ — firewalled on both sides, sitting between internet and internal network.

1.title: System Security Risks
1.text: The DMBOK catalogs several system security risks along with their mitigations. Abuse of excessive privilege is when users have more access than they need; you mitigate it with query-level access control. Abuse of legitimate privilege is when users misuse access they're entitled to, intentionally or accidentally; you mitigate it with endpoint access control. Unauthorized privilege elevation is exploiting vulnerabilities to gain admin rights; you mitigate it with intrusion prevention plus query access control. SQL injection is injecting unauthorized SQL into data channels, and you mitigate it by sanitizing inputs. Default passwords are known to hackers, so eliminate all of them after every implementation. And backup data is itself a risk, so encrypt all database backups. The mitigation most likely to be tested: sanitize inputs to stop SQL injection.

1.title: Malware & Social Threats
1.text: Let's cover malware and social threats. Adware monitors your browsing habits — it's not illegal but is easily leveraged for identity theft. Spyware tracks online activity without consent, often piggybacking on other software. A Trojan horse is a malicious program disguised within legitimate software. A virus attaches to an executable file and needs a host program to run, executing when the infected file is opened. And a worm self-reproduces and spreads across a network on its own, consuming bandwidth and potentially shutting the network down. On the social side: phishing lures victims into revealing private information; spear-phishing is targeted at specific senior executives by name; and social engineering tricks people into granting access. The key malware distinction for the exam: a virus needs a host program, while a worm self-replicates without one.

1.title: The 5 Security Activities
1.text: Data Security has five activities. First, identify data security requirements — analyzing business rules and processes, using data-to-role and CRUD matrices, and building a central inventory of all relevant regulations. Second, define the data security policy — which is governed by the Data Governance Council, and which should be kept separate from, and more granular than, the IT security policy. Third, define data security standards — for example, requiring passwords to change every forty-five to one hundred eighty days, using two-factor authentication for highly sensitive information, and assigning confidentiality levels to all data elements. Fourth, implement controls and procedures — role-based access control, the CRUD matrix mapping create, read, update, and delete, and both active and passive monitoring. And fifth, audit data security — using auditors who are independent of the process being audited, with the goal of objective assessment, not fault-finding. Remember that independence requirement for auditors.

1.title: Outsourcing, Cloud & Metrics
1.text: A few closing topics. On outsourcing, the guiding principle is memorable: anything can be outsourced except liability. So while an outsourced partner may implement security, your organization must retain ownership of the security architecture, and you define responsibilities using RACI matrices in the contract. In the cloud, the as-a-service models — data, software, and platform as a service — require adapted security policies, and chain of custody and shared responsibility become critical, because your data may sit in a provider's cloud. Finally, the metric categories: security implementation, security awareness, data protection, security incidents, and confidential data proliferation — that last one being about reducing the number of copies of confidential data. The line to remember: you can outsource the work, but never the liability.

1.title: Key Numbers & Quick Facts (Cheat Sheet)
1.text: Let's consolidate. Data Security has three goals and two business drivers — risk reduction and business growth. The Four A's are access, audit, authentication, and authorization, plus entitlement. The three risk classifications are CRD, HRD, and MRD. There are five confidentiality levels, one per data set. Confidentiality is internal and singular; regulatory is external and additive. SOX governs who can change financial data; insider trading laws govern who can see it. HIPAA is health, FERPA is education, PCI-DSS is cards. Encryption is hash, symmetric with AES, or asymmetric with RSA. Masking is persistent for non-production or dynamic for production. And passwords change every forty-five to one hundred eighty days. Drill these.

1.title: Common Exam Traps
1.text: Here are the traps for this chapter. First, never confuse authentication with authorization — authentication proves identity, authorization grants privileges. Second, it's regulatory classification that's additive, not confidentiality; confidentiality is a single level per data set. Third, SOX controls who can change financial data, while insider trading laws control who can see it. Fourth, tokenization is not encryption — a token has no mathematical relationship to the original value, whereas encryption is a reversible cipher. And fifth, it's a worm that self-replicates, while a virus needs a host program. One more to carry: persistent masking is for non-production copies, and dynamic masking only changes the display. Nail these and you'll dodge the chapter's favorite tricks.

1.title: Module Summary
1.text: Let's wrap up. Data Security delivers the Four A's — authentication, authorization, access, and audit — at the Goldilocks level: appropriate, neither too lax nor too restrictive. It's metadata-driven, and classification using CRD, HRD, and MRD follows the aggregation rule, where the most sensitive item sets the level. There are five confidentiality levels, which are internal and singular, contrasted with additive regulatory categories — and remember SOX is change, insider trading is see. Encryption and masking protect data, and tokenization is distinct from encryption. Finally, the five activities run from identifying requirements through policy, standards, controls, and an independent audit. That's Chapter 7.

1.title: Let's Test Your Knowledge
1.text: Let's test your knowledge with five questions on data security. These focus on the distinctions we emphasized — who classifies data, the masking types, tokenization versus encryption, and access-control models. Read each one carefully, choose your answer, and then reveal the solution. Here we go.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one: who bears primary responsibility for classifying data assets? The answer is B — the Data Steward or Data Owner of the business domain, because they understand the business value and sensitivity of the data. Security and IT implement the controls, and the governance council sets policy, but the business owner drives the actual classification.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two: what distinguishes static, or persistent, masking from dynamic masking? The answer is D — static masking permanently transforms data in a copy of the dataset, while dynamic masking transforms the display at query time without altering the stored data. Watch out for option A, which reverses the environments.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three: a development team needs a sanitized copy of production for testing. Which approach? The answer is B — static data masking, creating a persistent masked copy for the test environment. Dynamic masking is for live production display, and re-identifiable tokens or mere encryption-at-rest would still expose real values to the test team. Two more on the next slide.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four: how does tokenization differ from encryption? The answer is A — tokenization replaces sensitive data with a non-sensitive surrogate token that has no mathematical relationship to the original, while encryption is a reversible algorithm recoverable with a key. A token is a meaningless stand-in; that's why compromising it reveals nothing. Note that option D reverses the two techniques. Question five: a healthcare organization grants access based on department, job title, time of day, and data sensitivity. Which access-control model? The answer is B — Attribute-Based Access Control, ABAC, because it evaluates multiple contextual attributes of the subject, resource, action, and environment. RBAC keys only on role, DAC on owner discretion, and MAC on fixed system labels — none of those handle the full mix of attributes the scenario describes. That completes Module 7. Next up is Module 8, Data Integration and Interoperability, where we'll cover ETL, ELT, and the movement of data across systems. I'll see you there.
